Self-Inductance

Any current-carrying loop creates a magnetic field, and that field produces a flux through the loop itself. If the current changes, the self-flux changes, and by Faraday’s Law, an EMF is induced in the loop. This phenomenon is called self-induction, and the proportionality constant between flux linkage and current is the self-inductance (or simply inductance) \(L\):

\[\boxed{L = \frac{N\Phi_B}{I}}\]

The SI unit is the henry (H), named after Joseph Henry:

\[1\ \text{H} = 1\ \frac{\text{Wb}}{\text{A}} = 1\ \frac{\text{V}\cdot\text{s}}{\text{A}}\]

The self-induced EMF is:

\[\boxed{\mathcal{E}_L = -L\frac{dI}{dt}}\]

The negative sign (Lenz’s Law again) means the induced EMF opposes the change in current. When current is increasing (\(dI/dt > 0\)), the inductor opposes the increase. When current is decreasing (\(dI/dt < 0\)), the inductor opposes the decrease. An inductor resists any change in current — it has electromagnetic inertia.

Inductance of a Solenoid

The solenoid is the archetype inductor, just as the parallel-plate capacitor is the archetype capacitor. For a solenoid with \(N\) turns, length \(\ell\), cross-sectional area \(A\), and turns per unit length \(n = N/\ell\):

The field inside is \(B = \mu_0 nI\) (from Chapter 28). The flux through each turn is \(\Phi_B = BA = \mu_0 nIA\). The total flux linkage is \(N\Phi_B = (n\ell)(\mu_0 nIA) = \mu_0 n^2\ell A I\). Therefore:

\[\boxed{L = \mu_0 n^2 \ell A = \mu_0 n^2 V}\]

where \(V = \ell A\) is the volume of the solenoid. This can also be written as:

\[L = \frac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{\ell}\]

The Grand Analogy — Inductor vs. Capacitor

This parallel is remarkable and worth studying carefully:

Property Capacitor (Ch 25) Inductor (Ch 29)
Stores energy in Electric field Magnetic field
Defining relation \(C = Q/\Delta V\) \(L = N\Phi_B/I\)
Geometry (ideal) \(C = \varepsilon_0 A/d\) (parallel plates) \(L = \mu_0 n^2\ell A\) (solenoid)
Energy stored \(U_E = \frac{1}{2}C(\Delta V)^2 = \frac{1}{2}\frac{Q^2}{C}\) \(U_B = \frac{1}{2}LI^2\)
Energy density \(u_E = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2\) \(u_B = \frac{1}{2}\frac{B^2}{\mu_0}\)
Opposes changes in Voltage (holds \(\Delta V\) constant) Current (holds \(I\) constant)
In DC steady state Open circuit (\(I = 0\)) Short circuit (\(\Delta V = 0\))
Characteristic equation \(I = C\,d(\Delta V)/dt\) \(\mathcal{E} = -L\,dI/dt\)
SI unit Farad (F) = C/V Henry (H) = V\(\cdot\)s/A

Both devices store energy in fields. The capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its plates; the inductor stores energy in the magnetic field inside its coils. The duality runs deep: every capacitor equation has an inductor counterpart with \(Q \leftrightarrow \Phi_B\), \(\Delta V \leftrightarrow I\), \(C \leftrightarrow L\), and \(\varepsilon_0 \leftrightarrow \mu_0\).

Example: Inductance of a Solenoid

A solenoid has \(N = 500\) turns, length \(\ell = 0.25\ \text{m}\), and radius \(r = 0.020\ \text{m}\).

Turns per unit length: \(n = N/\ell = 500/0.25 = 2000\ \text{turns/m}\)

Cross-sectional area: \(A = \pi r^2 = \pi(0.020)^2 = 1.26\times10^{-3}\ \text{m}^2\)

Inductance:

\[L = \mu_0 n^2\ell A = (4\pi\times10^{-7})(2000)^2(0.25)(1.26\times10^{-3}) = \boxed{1.58\ \text{mH}}\]

This is a typical laboratory inductor. Millihenrys are common in electronics; henrys are rare and require very large coils.

Example: Self-Induced EMF

The solenoid above carries current that changes at \(dI/dt = 200\ \text{A/s}\).

\[|\mathcal{E}_L| = L\frac{dI}{dt} = (1.58\times10^{-3})(200) = \boxed{0.316\ \text{V}}\]

This “back-EMF” opposes the current change. In a circuit with a 12 V battery, this is a modest effect. But if you try to interrupt a large current through an inductor very quickly (\(dI/dt \to\) very large), the back-EMF can be enormous — this is why opening a switch on an inductive circuit produces a spark. The inductor “fights” the sudden current drop by producing whatever voltage is needed to maintain current flow, even if that means arcing across the switch gap.

Mutual Inductance

When two coils are near each other, a changing current in one induces an EMF in the other. The mutual inductance \(M\) quantifies this coupling:

\[\mathcal{E}_2 = -M\frac{dI_1}{dt} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mathcal{E}_1 = -M\frac{dI_2}{dt}\]

where:

\[\boxed{M = \frac{N_2\Phi_{12}}{I_1} = \frac{N_1\Phi_{21}}{I_2}}\]

Here \(\Phi_{12}\) is the flux through coil 2 due to the current in coil 1. A remarkable theorem (the Neumann formula) guarantees that \(M\) is the same regardless of which coil is the source and which is the receiver.

The transformer is the most important application: two coils wound on a shared iron core with \(M\) close to its theoretical maximum. From Chapter 31, the voltage ratio equals the turns ratio: \(V_2/V_1 = N_2/N_1\). Transformers are why we can transmit electrical power over long distances — stepping up to high voltage for transmission (low \(I^2R\) losses) and stepping down for safe household use.
